seo.title: CSV and Excel import, XLSX export and backups
seo.description: Import CSV, JSON, Excel and SQL files, export tables and results to formats such as XLSX and Parquet, open data files alone, and back up with dump tools.

header.title: Import and export
header.lead: Import files into supported tables and export tables or query results. Open CSV, JSON and Excel files without a database connection.

sections.title: Import files into a table
paragraphs: Import {importFormats} files. Data formats use column mapping into existing or new tables; Excel imports the first sheet only. SQL files run as statements, including .sql.gz dumps and SQL Server scripts using GO.
Imports use one transaction unless disabled. Choose how to handle failed rows: roll back, keep imported rows or skip failures. Export skipped rows as CSV for review.

blocks.title: Saved mappings and encodings
paragraphs: Reuse saved column mappings for CSV, JSON and Excel. <ui>Match by Name</ui> maps named fields; <ui>Match by Position</ui> works for CSV and Excel. CSV and SQL also support UTF-16 and selected Japanese, Chinese and Korean encodings.

sections.title: Export tables and results
paragraphs: Export tables and views to {exportFormats}, streaming beyond the grid's row cap. SQL engines support per-table filters, limits and column selection. SQL exports can include structure; Excel uses one sheet per table. MongoDB supports mongosh-script export, not SQL export. Redis also has no SQL export.
<ui>Export Results</ui> reruns capped queries to stream the full result. Add {exportPluginFormats} export through a free plugin in <ui>Settings > Plugins</ui>, with one file per table.

blocks.title: Edit data files
paragraphs: Open and edit delimited text, JSON and JSON Lines as tables. Filter, search, replace text or remove duplicate rows. Excel sheets and compressed files such as .csv.gz open read-only.
Changes stay in a private copy until you save. Saving writes the original format and preserves untouched rows.

blocks.title: Column statistics, then export or import
paragraphs: Inspect empty and distinct counts, ranges and common values. Click a value to filter, then export the file or use <ui>Import into Table</ui> on an open connection.

sections.title: Backup and restore
paragraphs: Backup Dump and Restore Dump use {backupTools}, with the connection's SSH and TLS settings. Install the required command-line tool yourself, except for DuckDB, which writes its own database or Parquet dump.
Server-Side Export on {serverSideExport} writes through Oracle Data Pump, a Snowflake stage or Cloud Storage. The export stays off your Mac.

sections.title: Files that are databases
paragraphs: SQLite and DuckDB files open from Finder as connections. DuckDB also reads Parquet, CSV and JSON files as read-only views, so a .parquet file opens as a DuckDB connection rather than in Data Files. A SQLite database on an SSH server opens either live, through a small agent that needs Python 3.6 or later on the server, or as a read-only copy.
.sql files open as query tabs and save back to disk, and a Beancount ledger opens read-only as a set of tables.

sections.title: From one database to another
paragraphs: Copy or transfer tables between supported connections without an intermediate file. See Schema for type conversion and review details.

sections.title: On iPhone and iPad
paragraphs: The iPhone and iPad app copies or shares rows and query results as JSON, CSV or SQL INSERT statements, from the rows it has loaded. A copy stays on that device’s clipboard and is not shared with your other devices.

Rows go in through the Shortcuts actions Add Row to Table and Add Rows to Table, which take JSON or CSV text or a file and follow the connection’s Safe Mode. There is no import sheet, file export, Data Files window or backup on iPhone and iPad.

limits: A SQL export includes DROP TABLE IF EXISTS before each table unless you turn that off, so check the options before running the file against a database whose tables you want to keep.

Backup Dump uses command-line tools you install yourself, and only on the engines listed. The tools get the password through the environment or a temporary file. The exception is sqlpackage, which takes the SQL Server password on its command line, where other processes on the Mac can read it; TablePro asks before it starts.
Restore Dump replaces the tables in a MySQL or MariaDB dump. On the other engines it does not replace an object that already exists, and a SQL Server .bacpac needs an empty database.
Opening a database file over SSH works for SQLite only.
DuckDB extensions that are not built in, such as httpfs for S3, Iceberg and Delta, download from DuckDB’s own servers the first time a query needs them.
In the current App Store version, the Shortcuts actions read CSV and JSON only as UTF-8, and CSV only with LF line endings.
